en: Abhidhānottaratantra, Chapter 29 [Tibetan & Sanskrit 32] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition = 1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
[185.7] [1146'] Now I shall further explain the sequence of the yoga for accomplishment,
the supreme vow of the samaya through the yoga of the *ḍākas* and *ḍākinīs*.
The great bliss of all phenomena and the ḍākinīs;
the supreme samaya-maṇḍala situated in the center of the space-vajra-realm;
therein, in the middle, is the great wheel adorned with five maṇḍalas.
In the center is the beautiful solar seat,
endowed with the vowels and consonants, possessed of the thirty-two major marks and adorned with the eighty minor signs;
having established the stage of empowerment, it is produced from its own seed-syllable.
Born from the syllable *hīṃ*, terrifying like the fire of universal destruction,
with a mouth formidable with fangs, three-eyed, and licking [the corners of his mouth],
he stands treading upon all the wicked; full of wrath yet with a smiling face.
Trembling with the fire at the end of the eon, adorned with a crown of vajras,
standing in the ālīḍha posture, decorated with a garland of severed heads,
and remaining with his waist girt by the skin of Mahābhairava.
He wears a crown of garlands of skulls and the half-moon atop a double-vajra;
he has four arms and bears matted locks.
Furthermore, with a garland of vajras upon his forehead, he gazes with a wrathful look.
The great devourer of all gods, the observer of the kaṅkāla-vow,
the supreme reviver of the dead, and the subduer of all the wicked.
Adorned with the body-ornaments of the six mudrās and decorated with various jewels,
she has six arms and five faces, possessing the most excellent of diverse aesthetic sentiments (rasas). Her faces are blue, yellow, red, green, and white for the sake of peace.
He is in union with Vajraghaṇṭā; he is embraced by Vārāhī at his doorway; he wears a garment of a human skin like a spread-out canopy;
he holds a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a ḍamaru drum, and likewise a *yama*.
Having pressed down the two feet— Kālarātri with the left foot and Bhairava likewise with the right— she,
agitated and having caused them to lose consciousness,
is the same color as Vajravārāhī, with loose hair and naked.
Wearing a crown of garlands of skulls and a girdle adorned with fragments, she embraces his neck while encircling both his shanks; agitated, her hands bear his symbols:
the ritual knife and the hand-drum.
The sixth is the Brahmamuṇḍaka.
A wise person should place such a Vajraḍāka in the central compartment;
however, Buddhaḍāka is in the east, and Karmaḍāka is in the north.
The western [deity] is Padmaḍāka, while to the south are Ratnaḍāka and [the others].
They are white, blue, red, green, and yellow respectively;
they embrace the vajra and bell and stand in the ālīḍha posture.
Green, yellow, red, blue, and white from above;
with a bell and a crossed-vajra, he possesses true bliss embraced by the goddess;
he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture.
Red, blue, yellow, green, and white;
embracing the lotus and bell, and pressing against the breasts of the goddess—
yellow, blue, as well as red, green, and white.
Absorbed in the jewel-bell, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture;
likewise, these five ḍākas are indeed the five vows (*pañcasamvara*) located in the southeast,
southwest, northwest, and northeast.
Buddha-Ḍākinī, Ratna-Ḍākinī, Padma-Ḍākinī, and Karma-Ḍākinī; likewise, they have three faces and six arms,
possess three eyes, have loose hair, and are adorned with garlands of skull-cups.
Complete with all ornaments and adorned with the five mudrās,
they dance naked, adorned with garlands of severed heads,
bearing skull-cups and khaṭvāṅgas, having become Vajravārāhīs.
The auspicious Goddess, holding a noose and a goad, bestows all space; she is of beautiful form,
possessing a vajra-like nature, well-proportioned, having a vajra-beak, and radiating light.
Vaḍavāmukhī, Ghoremukhī, Vajraghoṇā, and Yaśasvinī.
Vajradṛtī, Vajranakhī, and likewise Vajrakaumārīkā; Kambojī, Vajravetālī, and Vajrasāyikā— these indeed.
Gandhārī, Bhīmavadanā,
Candraśekharī,
as well as Bhṛkuṭī, Viśvarūpī, and Vajrakātyāyanī.
Vajraśṛṅkhalikā, Māyādevī, Yaśaskarī,
Nalārki, Piṅgalā, [Vajrajvālinī], and Kuṇḍalī.
And Vajrabhairavikā herself, Siddhiḍākinī, is in the maṇḍala.
All these ḍākinīs have three eyes and distorted faces;
they have protruding bellies and loose hair, and are adorned with garlands of skulls.
Complete with all ornaments and adorned with the five mudrās,
they dance with naked bodies and are decorated with garlands of severed heads.
Mounted upon a corpse, she is the supreme goddess for all, possessing a universal form that is captivating, and holding a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a noose, and a goad.
Intent on the upward movement of the *vajra*, holding a bell and a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*).
She has three faces, possesses the heroic and erotic sentiments, and is filled with the sentiment of compassion.
Intent on side-long glances, she was restless with the breasts during amorous play.
She bestows all accomplishments and is devoted to the practitioner.
The practitioner accomplishes the wheel of ḍākinīs within six months.
Without doubt, one attains the supreme accomplishment, which is the state of having the form of Heruka.
In no time at all, one will undoubtedly attain the state of moving through the sky.
And in the inner enclosure, there should be nine compartments and so forth, provided with doors.
One should place four goddesses at the gates: Ḍākinī, who bestows accomplishment (siddhi).
One should indeed draw the deities on the outer mandala, as well as the strips [of cloth] in its four corners.
Having placed the twenty deities of the Goddess, as well as the Ḍākinīs, in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The outer mandala should be conceived as square with four gates.
At the gates are the four goddesses, who bestow the fruit of all desires.
Adorned with four gateways, decorated with necklaces and half-necklaces, and embellished with silk ribbons and garlands of flowers.
In all the corner sections and at the joints where the door-fills meet.
[... With these [measures], one should delineate the outer maṇḍala;
within that, there should be a grid of nine squares with doors.
Thus, through the ḍākinīs and ḍākas, one realizes the emptiness of the Jālasamvara.
Through purification, one perceives the true nature (*dharmatā*) within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
in the center, on the thirteenth stage, and externally, in the *pīṭhas*, *upapīṭhas*, as well as the *śmaśānas* and *upaśmaśānas*.
In this way, within the yogas of purification, one should cultivate the supreme vow.
Having recognized the increase of those [elements], the Jñānaḍāka and the Ḍākinī consist of the elements,
aggregates, and sense-bases, acquired through the two types of armor.
One should arrange the placement of the wheel of the three secrets, the supreme commitment of knowledge,
and the dance of the heroes and ḍākinīs within the centers of the groves.
Within the center of the wheel of the three eyes, this is the most wonderful commitment;
having drawn in that wheel of gnosis, one should employ the vessel of offering.
One should contemplate the consecration with the water of gnosis as the act of sovereign empowerment.

The single flavor of all phenomena, stainless and the supreme commitment; the radiance of the three secret commitments, pervading everywhere through the pores of the skin; the commitment of all sentient beings without exception, established in the sound of the ḍākas.
Having gathered that with agility, one should cause the triple secret to enter.
From the pre-established *viḍāka*, one should place the station of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhānapada*).
"Come, O Mahāyāna! You who abide in the way of conduct (*caryānaya*)."
One should indeed meditate upon the unsurpassed state to be recited as the recitation itself;
constantly, at the four junctions of the day, according to one's desire,
one should cause the supreme wheel-array to vibrate in both direct and reverse order.
Adorned with offerings, she should flash forth within the openings at the tips of the pores of the skin through the meditation on restraint by means of the triple wheel of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Accompanied by the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra), I shall recite [the mantra] which is filled like a cloud.

Through the practice of coming and going, the one with the vajra crown, the observer of the great vow (or the one of vajra silence), attains verified realization within seven nights; of this there is no doubt. Likewise, trembling, shaking, and the seventy types of supernatural manifestations occur.
It can make the painless painful, and it makes the painful painless;
this is accomplished through meditative cultivation— there is no need for hesitation here—
for those who are devoted to internal yoga and whose souls delight in recitation and meditation.

Free from doubt regarding the consumption of food at the appointed time and devoid of attachment to life, those whose intellects are firm and well-prepared should recite thus according to the ritual procedure.
Therein... [118 is missing].
He uttered the mantra for these [deities].
Oṃ śrīvajraḍāka āḥ hrīḥ hūṃ ḍākinījālasamvara hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrībuddha āḥ bhrūṃ hūṃ ḍākinījālasamvara hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrīkarmamaḍāka āḥ hūṃ khaṃ hūṃ ḍākinījālasamvara hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā ||
Oṃ śrīpadmaḍāka āḥ hrīḥ hūṃ ḍākinījālasamvara hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrīratnaḍāka āḥ trāṃ hūṃ ḍākinījālasamvara hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Among these, there are four: the ḍāka, the ḍākinī, as well as Rāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī.
Embraced by the neck, she has attained union, her body well-enveloped up to the knees.
One should visualize [the deity] as having the same color, arms, and faces as that [deity], like the expanse of space.
The heart-mantras are distinct from the goddesses who bring about their presence.
Oṃ śrīvajravārāhī vaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrīḍākinī ḍāṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrīrāme [Xṃ] hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrī khaṇḍaroge khaṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrīrūpiṇī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Thus, in the corners, there are the mantras of the fivefold ḍākinīs.
Oṃ śrī buddhaḍākinī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrī karmmaḍākinī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrī padmaḍākinī hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ śrī ratnaḍākinī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
At the gates are the mantras of the ḍākinīs, which bestow the fruits of all desires.
And the four universal castes are established according to their respective lineages.
Oṃ vajrarūpe hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ surūpe hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ vajratuṇḍī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ vajraprabhākarī hūṃ phaṭ!
On the front panel, the four goddesses have white bodies.
She uttered this mantra.
Oṃ vaḍavāmukhī hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ, O fierce-faced one, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
Oṃ vajraghoṇe hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ Yaśasvinī hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
On the southern panel, there are four goddesses of yellow color;
he spoke their mantra.
Oṃ vajradūtī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ vajranakhī hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ vajrakaumārī hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ vajrakāmbojī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
[119] The mantra for these [is as follows]:
Oṃ vajravetālī hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ vajrasāyike hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ vajragāndhāri hūṃ 2 phaṭ |
Oṃ, O you with the terrifying vajra face, hūṃ 2 phaṭ!
On the northern panel are four goddesses of green color.
He spoke their mantra:
Oṃ candraśekhare hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ bhṛkuṭī hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ viśvarūpe hūṃ 2 phaṭ ||
Oṃ vajrakātyāyanī hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
In the four corners starting from the northeast, there are four goddesses with two forms and colors.
He spoke this mantra for them.
Oṃ vajraśṛṅkhale hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ vajramāye hūṃ 2 phaṭ | Oṃ vajrayaśaskarī hūṃ 2 phaṭ |
Oṃ vajrānalārkī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
At the gates, he spoke the mantra of the four goddesses who possess fierce bodies of various colors: [first],
in the east.
Oṃ śrīvajrapiṅgali jaḥ hūṃ 2 phaṭ ||
In the south: Oṃ vajrajvālini hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
In the west:
Oṃ vajrakuṇḍali vaṃ hūṃ 2 phaṭ | [In the] north:
Oṃ vajrabhairavī hoḥ hūṃ 2 phaṭ |
One should join the syllable Śrī at the end of every *praṇava*. Following that in sequence,
the mantra practitioner should thus recite the *Siddhāḍākinījālasamvara*.
Within just six months, through the application of the state of silence, that great yogi is brought under control; thus the supreme Mahājāla is accomplished.
When ten million recitations of all mantras have been performed,
the kings of mantras are accomplished through the recitation of the supreme heart-mantra; one will become a hero, a *ḍākinī*, and an adept who acts according to his own will.
He attains the ability to enter the bodies of others and possesses four gates;
that great yogi may wander about, assuming various forms.
In the *Abhidhānottara*, the supreme *Samayasamvara*, this is the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Great Mandala King."
